items.title: GitLab Transcend Hackathon: Meet the 'Life After Code' winners
items.summary: Code generation is the easy part now. The hard part is everything that comes after it: getting software from a working change to running in production. That’s the problem we put to the community in the Transcend Hackathon: “Life after code, the path to production at the speed of imagination”.The hackathon, which ran during October, challenged participants to build agents and flows on GitLab Duo Agent Platform that can take over the work after the code is written. They also had to decide how much control to hand the agents, from approving every step to making them completely autonomous. More than 3,300 developers registered and 783 projects were submitted.The winning projects show how far agents and flows can go after code generation. A pharmacy app bug reported simply by shaking a phone was fixed and shipped in 18 minutes with no human in the middle. A teacher's email became a 3D-printable math graph a blind student could read by touch. A flow applied to a benefits software app helped detect payment miscalculations based on a won appeal. What these projects share: Agents do the reading, writing, and routing, while automated checks and people make the final calls.The winnersThe prize pool was $45,000 across nine categories, with each project eligible for one path prize and one special prize. You can find the full field in the project gallery.Path A: Start FreshNew projects built from scratch on GitLabBest Assisted Agent ($4,000): AftermathAftermath by Ahadi Cyizere answers the question scanners can't: When a hijacked npm package is disclosed, had it already run in last week's CI? A custom GitLab Duo flow with three subagents traces past CI jobs and the credentials each job could reach. A person signs off on the scope of the investigation, then on the containment plan, and finally closes the incident once CI has rotated only the exposed keys and deleted the affected images, and proof is attached.Best Supervised Agent ($4,000): LookbackLookback by Ujwal Suresh Vanjare and Arpita Madhukar Kalburgi starts from a won appeal. When benefits software gets the rules wrong for one person, a custom GitLab Duo flow triages the decision, reproduces the error with a failing test, and opens a fix merge request. After a person merges it, plain code replays past decisions to find every other household the bug affected and works out what each is owed. In the demo run, the replay found 413 underpaid households, and the amounts owed were published as a batch for the agency to pay.Best Hands-Off Agent ($5,000): ShakeFixShakeFix by Venkatesh Devale turns a phone shake into a production fix. A user of a pharmacy app shakes her phone and says what went wrong, and a GitLab Duo flow with four agents writes a failing test, fixes the bug, and checks the fix against production behavior side by side before it merges and deploys. In the team's live run, that process took just 18 minutes and 34 seconds with no human touches.Path B: Bring Your OwnExisting open source projects with agent-driven automation added and deployed on GitLabBest Assisted Agent ($4,000): UnstuckUnstuck by Aryan Shah and Riken Shah finishes the dependency upgrades that bots start but can't complete. A bot bumps a version number, but it can't read the release notes, fix what breaks, or decide what happens when behavior changes. Two custom GitLab Duo flows plan an upgrade campaign and carry it out one merge request at a time, quoting the release note behind every code change and stopping to ask a person when behavior would change. A daily monitor opens the next campaign when a new advisory appears. On doccano, an open source annotation tool stuck on an unsupported Django version with 80 known advisories, the campaign took the project to zero advisories and Django 5.2 in six reviewed merge requests.Best Supervised Agent ($4,000): CodeTinderCodeTinder by Jason Yu is built on a simple idea: review less code, teach agents more. On each merge request, a GitLab Duo agent picks one function and writes variants that pass the tests, and users swipe through the variants on their phone. The swipes update a versioned principles doc in the repo, which every agent reads, and an agent rewrites the rest of the merge request to match the updated doc.Best Hands-off Agent ($5,000): LocusLocus by Ahammad Shawki, Nourin Richi, and Mohammad Ashfaqul Hasan, built on the open source JSCAD library, lets a math teacher email a function in plain words and get back a tactile graph for a blind student. GitLab Duo agents design a raised-line graph with braille labels, check it against research-based touch rules for how fingertips read raised lines and braille, correct their own mistakes, publish the result on Google Cloud, send the print files to the teacher, and order the print graph. The agents can't mark their own work as ready to print; a graph is released only when it passes the touch rules.Special prizesThe Most Stages Covered prize goes to the projects that touch the most of the nine DevSecOp
